---
title: "Primer — Game-theoretic tools"
subtitle: "The conceptual building blocks used throughout the analyses"
---

This primer collects the formal tools the analyses reach for. Each tool gets one chapter; read in any order; cross-references flag where a primer chapter is needed for a given analysis.

The primer is descriptive, not prescriptive — it sets out what each model assumes, what it predicts, and *under what conditions it breaks*. The breaking conditions matter as much as the predictions: a tool's value comes from knowing where its assumptions fail.

## Primer chapters

### Foundational bargaining

- **[The bargaining model of war](bargaining-model.qmd)** — Fearon 1995, Powell 2006: when is war the rational outcome, and where does the model break?
- **[Audience costs and signaling resolve](audience-costs.qmd)** — Fearon 1994, Weeks 2008: democratic vs. autocratic, and why the IRGC institutional consensus is the binding audience in 2026 Iran.
- **[Two-level games](two-level-games.qmd)** — Putnam 1988: the international and domestic boards as one game; the win-set as the binding constraint on what Level-I bargains can survive ratification.
- **[Strategic ambiguity and threats that leave something to chance](schelling-strategic-ambiguity.qmd)** — Schelling 1960/1966: how rational actors generate credible threats by trading certainty for irreversibility — chokepoint risk, burned bridges, brinkmanship, focal points.
- **[Endogenous power shifts](endogenous-power-shifts.qmd)** — Fearon 1996, Krainin 2017, Bas & Coe 2016, Debs & Monteiro 2014, Chadefaux 2011: when bargaining itself moves the future power line — and the Q1.4 gap (the striker's prior actions causing the shift the canon treats as exogenous).

### Alliances, hierarchy, and coalitions

- **[Hierarchy and clientelism](hierarchy-clientelism.qmd)** — Lake 2009, Posen patron-client: when "alliance of equals" is the wrong frame, and why the framework swap from Olson-Zeckhauser was the project's most consequential analytical move.
- **[Omnibalancing and regime survival](omnibalancing.qmd)** — David 1991, Gause 2003/4, Reinhold 2001: when leaders balance internal threats over external ones, with Reinhold's three-pillar Saudi operationalization. The natural companion to Hierarchy and clientelism — Lake gives the external structure, omnibalancing gives the internal-threat dynamics.
- **[Hedging vs balancing vs bandwagoning](hedging-balancing-bandwagoning.qmd)** — Kuik 2016, Lim & Cooper 2015, Fulton 2026: what do Gulf states' actions actually fit? The third element of the Gulf analytical engine — categorizes the observable behavior the structural and internal-threat dynamics produce.
- **[Coalition theory and selectorate](coalition-theory-selectorate.qmd)** — Riker 1962, Bueno de Mesquita et al. 2003: who has to consent, and why some autocrats survive war losses that should bring them down. Selectorate vs winning coalition; the W/S ratio as regime-defining feature.

## Why the primer matters

Most of these tools were developed for different questions than the 2026 Iran war. Applying them to this case requires knowing what each was originally about and where the analogy survives or breaks. That work belongs here, not buried in the analyses.
